title: Stock Futures Edge Up After Dow's Third Straight Weekly Loss
excerpt: Index futures pointed to a modestly higher open early Monday as investors steadied after the Dow's worst week since March, with oil prices and the coming Trump-Xi summit setting the week's tone.
body:
• Index futures pointed to a modestly higher open early Monday — Dow futures up about 0.3%, S&P 500 futures up 0.4% and Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.6% around 1:40 a.m. EDT, according to TipRanks — after the Dow fell 1.7% last week.
  • The blue-chip index's weekly slide was its biggest since March and its third straight losing week, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq finished roughly flat.
  • Rising Treasury yields and Middle East tensions drove the pullback: the 10-year yield touched 5%, and Brent crude traded near $102 a barrel.
  • This week's calendar is crowded: a Trump-Xi summit in Washington on Thursday, UN General Assembly addresses, and earnings from Costco, General Mills and Darden Restaurants.

U.S. stock futures pointed to a modestly higher open in the early hours of Monday, September 21, as Wall Street looked to steady itself after the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.7% last week — its worst weekly performance since March and its third consecutive weekly decline. The bounce in futures was cautious rather than convincing, with investors bracing for a week dominated by geopolitics and a new round of signals on the American consumer.

A volatile week ends with the Dow at a three-month low

The Dow's slide last week capped a turbulent five sessions. Stocks tumbled Monday as leading artificial intelligence companies called for a slowdown in AI development, though software names surged in response. The market fell again Wednesday after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates and issued hawkish guidance, before rebounding broadly Thursday. The blue-chip index finished the week at a three-month low, marking its largest three-week decline since late March, according to Barron's.

The broader market held up better. The S&P 500 ended the week roughly flat and the Nasdaq Composite finished higher for the week, both closing above their 50-day moving averages, while the small-cap Russell 2000 shed 1.5%. Bond yields did much of the damage: the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5%, a level last seen around 2007 and near a 19-year high, while the rate-sensitive two-year yield climbed to 4.74%.

Oil and the Middle East add pressure

Energy was the other weight on sentiment. Brent crude traded near $102.27 a barrel and U.S. benchmark WTI near $98.30 in early Monday trading, as traders monitored developments in the Middle East following weekend attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthis. President Donald Trump warned of major developments in the U.S.-Iran conflict, keeping the risk of oil supply disruptions in focus. Expensive crude complicates the inflation outlook just as the Fed has resumed raising rates, a combination that tends to squeeze both corporate margins and household budgets.

On the earnings front, this week's reports from Costco, General Mills and Darden Restaurants will be read closely for what they reveal about consumer spending and business costs. With higher borrowing costs and elevated fuel prices, investors are watching whether shoppers are trading down — and whether companies can keep passing costs through.

What's next: Trump-Xi summit and the UN gathering

The main event for markets is Thursday's long-anticipated summit between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, held as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is expected to address the assembly on Tuesday and meet with Gulf leaders. The summit agenda covers tariffs, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and other economic issues. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of the summit as "successful." The U.S. and China have been in a holding pattern on trade since last year, with some tariffs still in effect but no further escalation in rhetoric.

Whether Monday's early futures gains survive the opening bell will depend on how those headlines develop — and on whether the bond market gives stocks any relief.
